newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Ramos sees no signs of recession.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Ramos sees no signs of recession.

text.p: South African director general of finance Maria Ramos said on Friday that growth would fall short of the 2.9 percent target for calendar 1997 at about 2.2 percent, but said she did not see any sign of a recession.
"The economy has slowed down, we anticipated that...but recession means negative growth and we are not looking at negative growth," Ramos told Reuters in an interview.

Economists have expressed alarm recently that the economy, faced with slowing agricultural output, sluggish consumer demand and signs that manufacturing output is tapering off, could be moving into a recession.
The country posted a negative annualised growth rate of 0.8 percent in the first quarter of 1997. The second quarter figure is due on August 26.

"We are looking at an economy that after four years of growth had to make an adjustment and that is what we are talking about. We are looking at a higher growth rate for the second half of the year. We don't see a recession," Ramos said.
She said the finance department had revised its growth assumptions in the June 1996 Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy to 2.2 percent from 2.9 percent for calendar 1997.
This was marginally higher than the Reserve Bank's revised July growth forecast of 2.0 percent for calendar 1997, down from 2.5 percent.
Ramos said the March budget forecast of 2.5 percent GDP growth in fiscal 1997/98 had not been altered.
"Given the balance of payments environment, given what we see is happening on the manufacturing side, we think 2.2 percent is probably going to be around the level for the calendar year.

"I think the trend in manufacturing is still showing a strong upward trend and that makes a difference. We expected the agricultural sector to slow down, which it did, but we are still seeing strong output growth on the manufacturing side," she said.
Economists, concerned that the country faces a recession, have criticised central bank governor Chris Stals for his reluctance to cut what have been described as punitive interest rates.
Stals has insisted he will not ease monetary policy until he is convinced there is a sustained downward trend in inflation, money supply and private sector credit extension.
Ramos said that while interest rate policy was the prerogative of the central bank, she did see scope for easing in the near term.
The Reserve Bank's key interet rate has been at 17 percent since November last year.
"Looking at the numbers and the fundamentals, I think there is potential for bringing interest rates down sometime in the near future, but that is up to the Reserve Bank," Ramos said.
Annual consumer inflation fell to 8.8 percent in June from 9.5 percent in May, while preliminary money supply growth rose 12.79 percent in June, down from 15.32 percent in May.
Private sector credit extension growth dipped only slightly to 16.39 percent year-on-year from 16.57 percent.

Ramos said if the indicators showed signs of a continuing downward trend and the Reserve Bank did not ease monetary policy, she would share the concerns that there were potentially negative consequences for growth.
"But (the Reserve Bank) knows what the economy is doing and we will see a positive response on the interest rate side," Ramos said.
